To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the alpha5 helical region of the alpha-subunit of heterotrimer G proteins is a key structural determinant of GDP release and that this mechanism of activation is similar to the activation of small G proteins.
the alpha5 helices of the alpha-subunits of heterotrimer G proteins play a key role in the activation of G proteins by heptahelical receptors.
the alpha5 helical domain of the Galpha subunit plays a key role in the GDP release step in the activation of heterotrmeric G proteins.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structural basis of heterotrimer G protein activation.
the molecular mechanism of activation of heterotrmeric guanine nucleotide-binding proteins by heptahelical receptors and how this activation process is regulated.
the molecular mechanisms of G protein signaling and the development of novel therapeutics for diseases such as diabetes, cancer, cardiovascular disease, obesity and Alzheimer's.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the crystal structure of G-alpha(i1)-T29A shows substantial conformation changes in switch I and additional alterations in side chains that disrupt the coordination sphere of Mg(2+), which is bound to GDP.

the crystallographic structure of Galpha.i1 T329A provides a detailed molecular description for the mechanism by which the G protein alpha subunit is activated by a conformational change that is transmitted to the nucleotide binding site.
the alpha5 helical domain is a major determinant of the rate of basal G(i) activation and that this domain is critical for the activation of G(i) by receptor binding.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

heterotrimeric guanosine triphosphate-binding proteins (heterotrimeic guanosine 3',5' cyclic monophosphate-binding protein, or G proteins) couple to heptahelical (seven transmembrane helix) G-protein (heptahelical guanine nucleotide binding protein, or heterotrimeric) coupled receptors to relay extracellular (cell surface) signals to intracellular (inside the cell) signaling networks.
heterotrimeric and small G proteins have evolved to use similar mechanisms to release GDP.
we have provided structural evidence for a mechanism of heterotrimer G protein activation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the structural mechanism for GDP release from heterotrimeric and small G proteins appears to be similar.
the alpha5 helices of heterotrimer and small G proteins are structurally similar, suggesting a conserved mechanism for G protein activation.
the alpha5 helices of Galpha(i) proteins are important for G protein activation and that the mechanism of G protein activation may be conserved between heterotrimeric and small G proteins.
